frames.narration: It is 02:00 on a Wednesday. The scheduler starts the incremental backup of database orders-17, which holds 400 GB. Its full backup is on Sunday, and the scheduler staggers fulls so that only about one seventh of the fleet takes one on any day.

The agent asks for the blocks changed since the previous backup. About 5% of the database changed, so that is 20 GB instead of 400 GB. The throttle caps reads at 40 MB/s, so the read takes about 500 seconds, roughly 8 minutes, and the agent slows further if query latency rises.

The agent compresses the 20 GB to about 6.7 GB, which is a ratio of 3, encrypts it with the database's key and writes it to backup storage with a checksum. It also records the backup in the catalog as part of the chain that starts with Sunday's full.

The new backup is queued for copying. The copier, which may only write, puts it in the vault in the second region, in a separate account, with an object lock of 35 days that nobody can shorten. Deletes in the primary region are never replicated to the vault.

On its schedule the restore tester takes the newest chain from the vault, restores it into a scratch instance, replays the log, and checks it. The restore of 400 GB plus the 60 GB of three incrementals takes 38 minutes at 200 MB/s, and every check passes: checksums, the engine's consistency check, row counts and application queries.

Weeks later an attacker who has been inside for two days holds an administrator login for the production account. He encrypts orders-17 and tries to delete every backup. The copies in primary backup storage are gone, because they were in reach of the stolen login.

The same attacker tries the vault. It is in another account that the stolen login cannot assume, and its objects are locked in compliance mode, so the delete is refused and raises an alarm. The vault still has every backup from the last 35 days.

The team restores the newest chain that the tester marked clean, which is the one from before the first encrypted write, and replays the log up to just before that write. The database is back in 41 minutes, about 4 minutes of data are lost, which is within the targets of its tier 1: an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 4 hours.
